The Risk and Benefits of Living Near Volcanoes.

Today we will be looking at why people would risk their lives to live near a volcano. Is it really worth it?

Lesson Objective: Students should be able to assess the risk and benefits of living near a volcano.

Sparking Curiosity

Case Study: Mount Etna


 * an active stratovolcano on the east coast of Sicily, Italy
 * it lies above the convergent plate boundary of the African plate and the Eurasian plate
 * the tallest volcano in the European continent at 3329 metres
 * in June 2013, it was added to the list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites
 * it supports extensive agriculture with vineyards spread across the lower slopes of the mountain
 * its most recent eruption was on 15 May 2015 (VIDEO)

A volcano in my own backyard?


 Gathering Data & Exercising Reasoning

SCENARIO

You are given a choice to migrate to Sicily, Italy and live in one of the houses seen in the photograph.

In order to make a decision, you have decided to find more information regarding the risk and benefits of living near an active volcano.

Sources of information for real-life examples of volcanic eruptions:

 1. Case Study of Chances Peak, Montserrat
 2. Case Study of Mount St Helen 
 3. Benefits from the eruption of Mount Pinatubo and Mount St. Helen.
 4. Any reliable news articles (e.g. BBC, CNN, NY Times, Reuters, The Telegraph) on a volcanic eruption.
 5. News reports on Youtube.


Post all your evidences here:

 * Risks of living near volcanoes
 * Benefits of living near volcanoes

Exercising Reasoning

In your groups, write a report to justify your decision to migrate or not to migrate to Sicily, Italy. Each group to produce 1 report onto primarypad.

You may use the structure of your open ended 8m essay question for you report and refer to Textbook pg. 39-42. Use the collated examples on padlet to support your answer.

10 ridiculously beautiful places in Europe to add to your bucket list immediately

Europe is filled with breathtaking hotspots from the Plitvice Lakes National Park in Croatia to Iceland's iconic Blue Lagoon

Europe is filled with spectacular landscapes, from rolling green hills to towering mountains, spectacular sandy shores to winding rivers surrounded by picture-perfect scenery.

The sheer abundance of destinations can make trying to plan a holiday somewhat daunting - but now, thanks to Eurochange, we've just got a massive dose of travel inspiration.

That's because the foreign exchange experts have narrowed down the list to the top 10 most incredible natural landmarks in Europe.

To determine the list, they analysed TripAdvisor data including the number of reviews and the average score for each landmark to determine which ones are proving particularly popular with visitors.

Plitvice Lakes in Croatia came out on top thanks to its ethereal terraced lakes and lush green landscape, closely followed by Iceland's iconic blue lagoon which has been a hit with tourists for decades.

Would you make an ACTIVE volcano part of your Mediterranean holiday? | Travel News | Travel

WHEN you think of Italy, you might think of beautiful towns with cute cobbled streets.

09:07, Fri, May 13, 2016 Updated: 09:37, Fri, May 13, 2016

Getty

There are three active volcanoes in Italy

You picture floating gondolas in Venice or luscious hills in Tuscany.

It’s the place that tourists visit for some rest and relaxation and beautiful food and wine.

But Italy is also home to three of the most active volcanoes in the world.

Italy has a fiery side to it and you get up close and personal with all three active volcanoes.

Getty

Mount Stromboli erupting

Getty

Mount Stromboli is on an island off the coast of Sicily

Mount Stromboli is actually on a small island north of Sicily, one of the most popular holiday destinations in Italy.

It brings in the crowds day after day, despite the fact that it’s still very active - the last major eruption was in 2009.

It’s actually been erupting continuously for 2000 years.

Visitors can actually get very close to the action but the easiest way to experience the volcano is actually as part of an evening tour.

They’ll pick you up, take you for an early dinner and then you’ll make your way to the viewing points to watch Stromboli work its magic at night, when it lights up the sky.

Getty

Mount Etna erupts almost every year

Getty

A view of Mount Etna

At 10,922 foot above sea level, Mount Etna is actually the tallest of Italy’s active volcanoes.

And it’s been active recently. The last eruption was in December 2015. But this isn’t a surprise to locals or experts - it erupts around once every two years. Except for a lucky escape for 2007, the volcano has erupted once a year for the last 15 years.

So why not take a trip to see mount Etna in all its glory? People still take a trip to the top of the volcano despite the frequency in which it erupts.

That’s not nearly as dangerous as the daredevils who bungee jump into an volcano in Chile.


Volcano bungee jumping in Chile

Getty

Pompeii was destroyed by Mount Vesuvius

Getty

Mount Vesuvius in Naples

Mount Vesuvius, Naples

Mount Vesuvius is Europe’s only mainland volcano and thanks to its history, probably the most famous.

Its best-known eruption was in AD 79 when it decimated the town of Pompeii. Volcanic ash spewed 30 kilometres into the air and the eruption actually pushed the line of the coast back several kilometres.

Since AD 79 it has erupted a total of 30 times and although the most recent explosion was in 1944, it's still considered to be an active volcano.

The volcano could erupt at any time but despite the dangers, 2 million people visit the area each year and you can climb to the top of the volcano and peek into the crater.
